label: HMRC update · 19 November 2026
title: Over 100,000 companies a year file their Company Tax Return more than 12 months late: what directors should know
summary: HMRC says more than 100,000 companies a year file their Company Tax Return over a year late. Returns are due even when there is no tax to pay, and directors stay legally responsible.
body:
In its Agent Update published on 19 November 2026, HMRC included a bulletin for Corporation Tax agents and advisers about late Company Tax Returns. The figures are striking, and the message applies to every limited company director.

What HMRC says

  • More than 100,000 companies a year file their Company Tax Return more than 12 months late.
  • In May 2026, over 20,000 companies had returns that were more than a year overdue.
  • A return is due by the statutory deadline even if the company has no tax to pay, and penalties may apply if it is late.

What happens if a return is not filed

If no return is received, HMRC may issue a determination. This is HMRC's estimate of the Corporation Tax it thinks the company owes. HMRC is clear that a determination does not replace the company's own obligations: the company must still file its return and pay any tax due, together with interest and penalties.

Directors remain responsible

HMRC points out that while accountants and agents help companies meet their obligations, the company and its directors remain legally responsible. Having an accountant does not move that responsibility away from the board.

If your company has stopped trading

A common reason returns go missing is that a company has quietly stopped trading. HMRC says directors of companies that have stopped trading should:

  • tell HMRC promptly;
  • file any outstanding returns; and
  • where appropriate, apply to dissolve the company through Companies House (form DS01).

Leaving a dormant or finished company on the register without dealing with HMRC can lead to penalties and determinations building up.

What HMRC advises for outstanding returns

HMRC's advice is that companies with outstanding returns should file them to avoid further late-filing penalties, determinations and compliance checks.

What I would do now

  • Check your company's HMRC online account for any Company Tax Returns that are shown as outstanding, including for earlier periods.
  • Confirm your company's accounting periods, so you know which returns HMRC expects.
  • If the company has stopped trading, do not just leave it. Tell HMRC, bring the filings up to date and decide whether to close it.
  • If you have received a determination, do not treat it as the final bill. File the actual return.

If your company is behind with its Company Tax Returns, or you have a company you no longer use, get in touch. We can bring the filings up to date and, if you want, close the company properly.
